children.author: refactor_master
children.text:
Same experience trying to find any kind of fashion object. I’d expect it to scour the internet, learn from patterns, understand fashion trends…

“Here’s a a list that includes some generic brands because their About page vaguely shares your ideals and a pop-up that closed in 2023”

It does not read their SoMe, it does not read their listings, hell, Gemini of all bots should know when a shop doesn’t exist on Google Maps any longer.

The world outside self-validating code is completely different.

Over the past week, I have been looking for an affordable handheld wood plane. So let's look at this quote:

> the first step toward mass adoption by the public of a technology that would fundamentally change purchasing habits. ... This is possibly the last Black Friday as we know it

I'm using ChatGPT, Sol 6.1. My requirements are fairly simple: a 45 degree blade, approx Stanley #5 style (so about 35cm long), I would prefer wooden handles but not required, must be affordable for a 'first' plane, not an expensive expert's tool, so sub-100-euros: find me one in a store I can order locally (Estonia, known for its online tech in general, you order everything online.)

It turns out finding one that length at that price is hard.

But the experience of AI-assisted shopping has been infuriating and frustrating.

It kept circling back to other planes than my requirements. It frequently recommended shops and listings, when the listing page itself notes something as out of stock: I did a lot of manual checking. It constantly links to index pages (eg an 'all hand tools' page) instead of an actual listing. It says what it could do (it could find workworking forums and see what people discuss) but doesn't actually do that. I ended up writing in all-caps to be diligent, to stop telling me what it could do and actually do it, to give it a goal like 'find five planes and their product pages; be recursive and dig into each page not just report a listing'.

Some of this may be me - it's been a busy week, I didn't want to guide ChatGPT like I do with coding architecture (where I co-work with an AI.) I got annoyed at circles and changing requirements, some of which may have been genuine issues it had meeting my requirements. And Codex is, in my view, significantly more proactive and intelligent than ChatGPT; perhaps I was using the wrong app.

For all that, I did find one I want to order.

But I can't imagine handing it my credit card. Not yet.

children.author: pm215
children.text:
This is almost certainly the result of this article being a rehash of some quotes from a radio interview. The interviewee is trying to communicate "this is safe", not give technical information. Unfortunately the FCA doesn't seem to have anything more specific I can find on their website at the moment (I was hoping for a press release at least), so the below is just speculation.

My guess is that what happens here is that you can tell your bank account (which you select and authenticate to via the bank's app or equivalent web UI) to authorize some specific AI agent for payments with given limits, without ever giving the agent direct information like "my sort code / account number" or "my banking password". So you have the guarantee at the bank end that even if the agent goes off down some weird sidequest it can't exceed the limitations and you can always disconnect it again at the bank's end. Something like the existing "pay by bank" mechanism https://www.openbanking.org.uk/pay-by-bank/ (which lets you say "pay this from my account with $BANK as a bank transfer" in a relatively smooth way without giving the merchant your bank info), but without the "for a specific amount" part that currently has, would be my suspicion.

“Without sharing banking details” but the Papa John’s agent had “permission to access their bank account and request payment to the retailer’s account.”

What identifies the correct account in this request? How is permission verified?

“J Chisel ordered $150 of pizza, please pay.” - so now the bank guesses which account holder (John Chisel? Jack Chisel? Jagged Chisel?) and which account (personal debit 2, personal debit 1, personal debit 4, savings, custodial savings, investment) to draft and *poof* money gone?

Don’t like it.

children.author: fenchurchstreet
children.text:
Potentially an unpopular opinion but i think it's silly that we're trying to shoehorn programmatic/"agentic" payments into a financial system that doesn't even let you run a banking app on a phone running GrapheneOS, when we already have cryptocurrency as an open-source, programmatic way of transacting value.

I'm a huge fan of stuff like the recently-mentioned x402 protocol (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50477649). We should be building on top of the programmer-friendly financial system we already have and develop more things to spend it on that are actually useful (ie. https://xmrtickets.com for train tickets), rather than inventing yet another payment method.

Really hoping that AI agent stuff leads to an increase in crypto usage ("free software money"), it's much simpler and the technology is already here.
